newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open lower amid profit-taking.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open lower amid profit-taking.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries opened lower on Monday as investors took a few profits after Friday's advance.
The 6-1/2 percent 30-year bond was down 8/32 to 101-20/32, yielding 6.38 percent in early trade.
On Friday, its yield fell to 6.36 percent, the lowest level since its March 4 close of 6.34 percent.
"All the press reports of a very healthy start to the Christmas spending season are helping to encourage some profit-taking," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A.
"The extent of Friday's run-up, which was related to month-end factors, left the market open to profit-taking as well," said Stiles.
"You have to find out if there is follow-through buying once those month-end factors are out of the way," he said.

Stiles said some players might have been reluctant to short the market in the midst of month-end portfolio adjustments, but now that those have passes, "they might be more inclined to adjust their positions."
Analysts said the market's focus is now on the NAPM (National Association of Purchasing Management) report.

"The market is kind of braced for a 50 to 51 type number with no price pressures emerging either," said Stiles. "But even if you get a surprising rise, you still have to take into consideration that all the longer term surveys like APICS and Dun and Bradstreet show expecations for manufacturing are lower."
Economists polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that the NAPM index would edge up slightly to 50.8 in November from 50.2 in October.
A stronger-than-expected NAPM reading would would encourage a little more profit-taking and shake out some players, but it would "not turn things around in a big way," said Stiles.

At 1000 EST/1500 GMT, the same time that the market gets the NAPM report, the government will also release figures on October construction spending. Economists polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that construction spending fell 1.0 percent during that month after September's 1.9 percent rise.
The week ahead is peppered with second-tier data leading up to the crucial monthly payroll employment report on Friday.
Economists estimate, on average, that payrolls expanded by 179,000 jobs in November, according to a Reuters poll.
"You have potential for a re-evaluation of what the market's done recently after the payroll number," said Stiles.
"The consensus is for a below-trend rise (in payroll growth), about 170,000 to 180,000 new jobs when trend is about 200,000," said Stiles.

Other aspects of the November employment report will also be important to the market. If the unemployment rate reaches a new cyclical low of five percent or 5.1 percent, that would likely revive the issue of how tight the labor market is.
"That's the kind of debate that would limit the market's gains and could shake a few people out," said Stiles.
